prompt: Match each word to its meaning.

right.text: A flip over a mirror line
A slide, with no turning or flipping
A turn around a fixed point
Shapes that fit together with no gaps or overlaps

hints: Think: flip, slide, turn.
solution: Reflection: a flip. Translation: a slide. Rotation: a turn. Tessellation: a pattern of shapes with no gaps or overlaps.

prompt: Which transformation turns a shape around a fixed point?

feedback.b: A reflection flips a shape over a mirror line.
feedback.c: A translation slides a shape without turning it.
feedback.d: A tessellation is a pattern of shapes, not a way of moving one shape.

hints: Think of the wheels on a bike.
solution: A **rotation** turns a shape around a fixed point, called the centre of rotation.

prompt: What do we call the line that a shape is reflected in?
hints: When you look in one of these, you see your reflection.
solution: It is called the **mirror line**.

prompt: How many degrees are in a half turn?
hints: A full turn is 360°.
solution: A half turn is half of 360°: **180°**.

prompt: A quarter turn is [[a]]°. A half turn is [[b]]°. A full turn is [[c]]°.
hints: Start with the full turn, then halve it, then halve it again.
solution: Full turn: **360°**. Half turn: **180°**. Quarter turn: **90°**.

prompt: The minute hand of a clock moves from 12 to 3. What turn has it made?

feedback.b: Clock hands always move clockwise. That is where the word comes from.
feedback.c: A half turn would take the hand from 12 to 6.
feedback.d: A three-quarter turn would take the hand from 12 to 9.

hints: 12 to 6 is a half turn. How far round is 12 to 3?
solution: 12 to 3 is one quarter of the way round the clock, in the direction clock hands move: **a quarter turn clockwise** (90°).

prompt: Select **all** the things that stay the same when a shape is reflected, translated or rotated.

options.text: Where it is on the page

hints: A transformation moves a shape. Does it stretch or squash it?
solution: Transformations only move a shape, so its **side lengths, angles, number of sides and size** stay the same. Its position on the page changes.

prompt: Sam is asked to translate a shape 4 squares to the right. He draws the image with 4 empty squares between the shape and the image. What has Sam done wrong?

options.text: He has moved it too far. He should count 4 jumps of one corner, not 4 empty squares.
Nothing. Leaving 4 empty squares is correct.
He should have flipped the shape over as well.
He should have moved it 4 squares up instead.

feedback.b: The empty squares don’t count the whole move. The shape’s own width gets added on, so it moves too far.
feedback.c: A translation is a slide. It never flips the shape.
feedback.d: "To the right" means across, not up.

hints: Pick one corner of the shape. How far should that corner move?
solution: In a translation every corner moves the same distance. Each corner should move **4 squares right**. Counting empty squares between the shapes adds the shape’s width, so the image ends up too far away.

prompt: In a tessellation, which of these is **not** allowed?

feedback.b: Rotating shapes is fine in a tessellation.
feedback.c: Reflecting shapes is fine in a tessellation.
feedback.d: A tessellation can use more than one shape, as long as they fit with no gaps or overlaps.

hints: Think of the tiles on a bathroom floor.
solution: A tessellation must have **no gaps** and no overlaps. Turning, flipping and using more than one shape are all fine.

options.text: Reflect in the mirror line, then translate 3 squares down
Reflect in the mirror line only

feedback.b: B is a mirror image of A, so there must be a reflection too.
feedback.c: A reflection alone would keep B at the same height as A. B is lower.
feedback.d: A turned shape is not a mirror image. B is a mirror image of A.

hints: Is B a mirror image of A?
Is B at the same height as A?
solution: B is a mirror image of A, so A was **reflected** in the mirror line. B is also 3 squares lower, so the image was then **translated 3 squares down**.

prompt: Which regular shape does **not** tessellate on its own?

feedback.b: Four squares fit around a point: $4 \times 90° = 360°$.
feedback.c: Six triangles fit around a point: $6 \times 60° = 360°$.
feedback.d: Three hexagons fit around a point: $3 \times 120° = 360°$.

hints: The corners that meet at a point must add up to 360°.
solution: Each corner of a regular pentagon is 108°. $3 \times 108° = 324°$ leaves a gap and $4 \times 108° = 432°$ is too much. So the **regular pentagon** does not tessellate on its own.

prompt: Bees build honeycomb from cells shaped like regular hexagons, with no gaps between them. Each corner of a regular hexagon is 120°. How many hexagons meet at each point?
hints: The angles around a point add up to 360°.
solution: $360 \div 120 = 3$, so **3** hexagons meet at each point.

prompt: One square tile and two regular octagon tiles meet at a point. Each corner of the square is 90° and each corner of an octagon is 135°. What is the total of the angles at the point?
hints: Add one square corner and two octagon corners.
solution: $90 + 135 + 135 = 360$, so the total is **360°**. The tiles fit around the point with no gap.

prompt: Ruby rotates a shape a quarter turn clockwise, then another quarter turn clockwise about the same point. Which single turn does the same thing?

feedback.b: Two clockwise quarter turns can’t add up to one turn the other way.
feedback.c: A full turn is four quarter turns.
feedback.d: A three-quarter turn is three quarter turns.

hints: Add the two turns: 90° + 90°.
solution: $90° + 90° = 180°$, which is **a half turn**.

prompt: Put these steps for reflecting a shape on a grid in the right order.

items.text: Pick one corner of the shape.
Count how many squares that corner is from the mirror line.
Count the same number of squares on the other side of the line and mark a dot.
Do the same for every other corner.
Join the dots to draw the image.

hints: You can’t join the dots until you have marked them all.
solution: Pick a corner, count its distance from the line, mark the same distance on the other side, repeat for every corner, then join the dots.

prompt: Describe the difference between **reflecting** a shape and **rotating** it.
modelAnswer: Reflecting flips the shape over a mirror line, so the image is a mirror image that faces the opposite way. Rotating turns the shape around a fixed point (the centre of rotation), so the image is the same shape turned around, not a mirror image.

rubric.criterion: Says a reflection flips the shape over a mirror line (making a mirror image)
Says a rotation turns the shape around a fixed point

hints: One of them is a flip and one is a turn.
What does each one need: a line or a point?
solution: A reflection is a flip over a mirror line and makes a mirror image. A rotation is a turn around a centre of rotation, and the image is not a mirror image.

prompt: Mia translates a shape 3 squares right. Then she translates the image 5 squares left. Which single translation does the same thing?

feedback.b: The two moves go in opposite directions, so they partly cancel out.
feedback.c: It moves further left (5) than right (3), so it ends up to the left.
feedback.d: The moves go in opposite directions, so you subtract, not add.

hints: Moving right then left partly cancels out.
Which move is bigger?
solution: 3 right and then 5 left: the 5 left cancels the 3 right and leaves **2 squares left**.

prompt: Which statement about rotating a shape a **half turn** is true?

options.text: It doesn’t matter whether you turn clockwise or anticlockwise.
The image is a mirror image of the shape.
The shape becomes twice as big.
Turning clockwise and anticlockwise give different images.

feedback.b: A rotation never makes a mirror image. Only a reflection does.
feedback.c: Transformations never change the size of a shape.
feedback.d: Half of a full turn is 180° either way, so you end up in the same place.

hints: A half turn is 180°. Picture turning 180° each way.
solution: A half turn is 180°. Turning 180° clockwise or 180° anticlockwise ends in the same place, so **the direction doesn’t matter**.

prompt: Tama is making a tile pattern. Around one point he has placed two regular hexagons (each corner 120°). He wants to fill the rest of the space with equilateral triangles (each corner 60°). How many triangles does he need?
hints: How many degrees do the two hexagons use?
The angles around a point add to 360°. How many 60° corners fill what is left?
solution: Hexagons: $120 + 120 = 240°$. Space left: $360 - 240 = 120°$. Triangles: $120 \div 60 = 2$. He needs **2** triangles.

prompt: Explain why regular pentagons can’t tessellate on their own. Each corner of a regular pentagon is 108°.
modelAnswer: Where the tiles meet at a point, the corners must add up to exactly 360°. Three pentagons make $3 \times 108° = 324°$, which leaves a 36° gap. Four pentagons would make 432°, which is too much, so they would overlap. 108 does not go exactly into 360, so regular pentagons can’t tessellate on their own.

rubric.criterion: States that the angles around a point must add up to 360°
Shows that 108° does not fit exactly into 360° (e.g. 3 × 108° = 324° leaves a gap, or 4 × 108° = 432° overlaps)

hints: What must the corners that meet at a point add up to?
Try 3 pentagons, then 4.
solution: The corners at a point must make 360°. Three pentagons give 324° (a gap) and four give 432° (an overlap). 108° doesn’t go exactly into 360°, so pentagons can’t tessellate on their own.

prompt: A shape is reflected in a mirror line that goes up and down. Then the image is reflected in a second mirror line that goes across. Which single transformation would give the same final image?

options.text: A half turn about the point where the two lines cross
A quarter turn clockwise about the point where the lines cross
One reflection in a different mirror line

feedback.b: Try it with a sketch: the final image is in the opposite corner, which a half turn gives.
feedback.c: A translation keeps the shape facing the same way. The final image here is upside down and back to front.
feedback.d: Two flips make the shape face its original way round again, so the result is not a mirror image of the start. It is a turn.

hints: Sketch it on squared paper with an L shape.
The first flip makes a mirror image. What does the second flip do to that?
solution: The first reflection flips the shape left to right. The second flips it top to bottom. Together the shape ends up in the opposite corner, upside down but not a mirror image: the same as **a half turn about the point where the lines cross**.
